hints: A string is a palindrome exactly when it equals its reversal.
A point change affects one position in both the forward and reversed representations.
Maintain polynomial hashes with a segment tree for both directions.
analogy: Compare a word seen from the left with the same word seen from the right.
example: Starting with abba, the full range is palindromic; changing the first a to c makes cbba, which is not.
algorithm: Store for each segment its length and forward and backward polynomial hashes. Merge adjacent segments by shifting one hash by the other segment's length. Update a leaf when a character changes; query the requested interval and compare its two hashes. Use two moduli or another robust hash to reduce collision risk.
correctness: The merge formulas represent exactly the forward and reversed strings of each interval. A palindrome always has equal hashes in both directions; equal hashes for different strings are possible but very unlikely with robust hashing.
complexity: For length n and q operations, O(n+q log n) time and O(n) space. Hashing is probabilistic.
